pages.text: Most people, if you asked them where in the world you would find pyramids, would say Egypt. Some might say Sudan. A few might mention Mexico. Almost nobody would say Nigeria. But they should.

In the Udi highlands of Enugu State, in south-eastern Nigeria, there is a village called Nsude. For centuries, the Igbo people of Nsude built something extraordinary there: a collection of stepped, circular towers, rising in rings from the red earth. They called them shrines. The world calls them pyramids.

image.note: Map of Nigeria with Enugu State highlighted; arrow to Nsude village

pages.text: The Nsude pyramids are not what most people imagine when they hear the word pyramid. They are not triangular. They are not made of stone. They do not have sharp points reaching into the sky. Instead, they are circular. They are built from red mud and clay, packed tight and shaped by hand. They rise in steps, each ring smaller than the one below, like a tower of wide flat plates stacked one on top of another.

There are ten of them, arranged in two rows of five. They stand about two kilometres from the centre of Nsude village, in open ground on a hillside. When they were standing at their full height, each one rose to about six metres, roughly the height of two tall adults, one standing on the other's shoulders. At the base, the widest section measured about eighteen metres around.

image.note: Side-view cross-section of one pyramid showing circular stepped structure with measurements labelled

pages.text: At the very top of each pyramid, a wooden stick was placed upright. That stick was not decoration. It was a marker, a sign that this place was the home of something sacred. The pyramids were not built to impress travellers. They were not built to be admired from a distance. They were built for a purpose: to honour a goddess.

That goddess was Ala. Ala is one of the most important deities in Igbo belief. She is the goddess of the earth, the ground beneath your feet, the soil that grows food, the land where your ancestors are buried. The Igbo people understood that everything living depends on the earth. Ala was the power that made that possible.

image.note: Illustration of earth cross-section: crops growing above, roots below, sky above

pages.text: To honour Ala, the people of Nsude built her a home. Not one home. Ten homes. The pyramids were shrines, sacred places where the community could bring offerings, perform rituals, and stay close to the goddess who sustained their lives. Each pyramid was believed to be a place where Ala could reside. The wooden stick at the top marked where the goddess sat.

The pyramids were not built once and left to stand forever. Mud and clay do not last the way stone does. Every rainy season, the rains softened the walls and wore away the surface. Every year, the community returned to rebuild, adding new mud, reinforcing the steps, replacing what the weather had taken. The pyramids were not monuments. They were living structures, maintained, repaired, and renewed by each generation.

This is something that separates the Nsude pyramids from the pyramids of Egypt. The Egyptian pyramids were built of stone and were meant to last forever without being touched again. They were tombs, places for the dead. The Nsude pyramids were built of mud and were meant to be renewed. They were shrines, places for the living.

image.note: Side-by-side diagram: triangular stone pyramid labelled Egypt / tomb / permanent; circular mud pyramid labelled Nigeria / shrine / renewed

pages.text: The first European to record the Nsude pyramids was the British anthropologist G. I. Jones. In 1935, Jones was travelling through south-eastern Nigeria, photographing the people, buildings, and culture of the region. He came across the pyramids and took a series of photographs. Those photographs are now among the most important historical records of the site.

Jones's photographs raised a question that historians and archaeologists have been asking ever since: how old are they? The pyramids have never been scientifically dated. We do not know exactly when they were first built. What we do know is that by the time Jones photographed them in 1935, they had already been maintained and rebuilt across many generations. The Igbo oral tradition, the stories and knowledge passed down through speech, suggests that the pyramids are very old indeed.
Cross-reference: Who built the Nsude pyramids, and why? See Chapter Two.

The Igbo people are one of the largest ethnic groups in Nigeria. They have lived in south-eastern Nigeria for thousands of years. Their language, Igbo, has many dialects. Different communities in different areas speak it in slightly different ways, but they share the same deep roots of culture, belief, and tradition. The community of Nsude is one Igbo community among many. But their pyramids make them unique.

To understand why the people of Nsude built their pyramids, you need to understand Igbo belief. The Igbo people recognised many deities, supernatural forces that governed different aspects of the world. Ala was among the most powerful of them. She was not simply a goddess of farming, though she governed the harvest. She was not simply a goddess of death, though she governed the burial of ancestors. She was the source of everything that grew from the ground and everything that returned to it.

In Igbo belief, building a shrine to Ala was not a choice. It was a responsibility. The community needed Ala's blessing for crops to grow. They needed her protection to keep the land healthy. They needed her acceptance for the dead to rest peacefully in the earth. A shrine was the community's way of staying in relationship with Ala, of giving back to the force that made their lives possible.

Why did the shrine take the shape of a pyramid? This is one of the questions that makes the Nsude pyramids so fascinating. The circular, stepped form rising from the earth mirrors the shape of a hill, as though the builders were copying the contours of the land itself, creating something that looked as though it had grown from the ground rather than been built on top of it.

image.note: Sketch: natural hill beside a stepped circular pyramid showing visual similarity in silhouette

pages.text: The structure of each pyramid also had a practical purpose. The central shaft, the hollow core running up through the centre of the pyramid, was the most sacred space. This was where offerings were placed: food, objects, and other gifts for Ala. The stepped exterior allowed people to approach the shrine, climb to different levels, and perform rituals at different heights.

Who actually did the building? In Igbo communities, large communal projects, including building, farming, and clearing land, were carried out collectively. The whole community contributed. The Nsude pyramids were not built by slaves, as some large ancient monuments were. They were not built by a ruler commanding workers. They were built by a community doing something they believed in together.

The Nsude pyramid community also had a guardian figure, a legendary ancestor called Uto-Nsude. In local tradition, Uto-Nsude was a great warrior and leader who, after his death, became a deity of the community. Some accounts suggest that the pyramids were originally built in his honour, before becoming the principal shrine of Ala. This layering of meaning, warrior ancestor, earth goddess, community shrine, reflects the depth and complexity of Igbo spiritual life.

The pyramids were central to Nsude community life for generations. They were not a tourist attraction or a heritage site. They were a living religious site, the place where the community turned in times of harvest, drought, illness, and loss. People came to the pyramids to pray, to offer gifts, to ask for Ala's help, and to give thanks when she provided it.

Each generation had a responsibility to the pyramids: to rebuild what the rains had worn away, to maintain what their parents and grandparents had maintained before them. This cycle of building, weathering, and rebuilding was not seen as a problem. It was part of the relationship between the community and their goddess. The pyramids were renewed because the relationship itself needed to be renewed, year after year, generation after generation.

The Nsude pyramids existed at the intersection of architecture, religion, community, and time. They were not static objects. They were something more like a continuous act, a practice performed across centuries, taking the same form again and again, each rebuilding an act of devotion. This is why calling them simply pyramids misses what makes them extraordinary.

image.note: Timeline diagram: repeated arc showing cycles of building and rebuilding across generations

pages.text: The pyramids are also evidence. They are evidence that the people of south-eastern Nigeria, long before any European arrived in the region, were capable of conceiving, planning, and building large, complex structures for purposes they understood clearly.

For much of the colonial period, the history and achievements of African peoples were ignored, dismissed, or deliberately erased by European colonial authorities. The Nsude pyramids are a concrete rebuke to that erasure. They stood as proof of an ancient, sophisticated, and deeply considered civilisation in the heart of what is now Nigeria.

They also raise a question that no historian has yet been able to answer with certainty: how old, exactly, are they? Without carbon dating, we cannot know precisely when the first pyramid at Nsude was raised. We know the community was still maintaining them in 1935. We know the tradition reaches back many generations before that. Some researchers believe they could be among the oldest pyramid structures in Africa outside Egypt and Sudan. That claim has not yet been proven. But it has not been disproven either.
Cross-reference: How were the Nsude pyramids built? See Chapter Three.

The Nsude pyramids were built from the land itself. No stone was quarried. No timber was felled for structure. The builders used what was directly beneath their feet: red earth, clay, and grass. This was not a limitation. It was a choice, and it reflects a sophisticated understanding of local materials and how to use them.

The method was called walling. The builders began by marking out a large circle on the ground. Then they dug a shallow circular trench along that line: a foundation. Into the trench they packed a mixture of red earth, clay, and dried grass. The grass acted as a binding agent, holding the clay together the way iron rods reinforce concrete in modern construction.

image.note: Cross-section of foundation trench showing layers of earth, clay, and grass with labels

pages.text: Once the first ring of the base was in place, the builders added the next layer, slightly smaller in circumference, set on top of the first. Then another layer. Then another. Each one smaller than the one below it, creating the stepped effect that gives the pyramids their distinctive profile. The walls were not poured. They were pressed and shaped by hand, section by section, each one left to dry in the sun before the next was added.

This process was slow. It required patience, precision, and collective effort. The circular form demanded that every section of wall be consistent in height and angle. A slight irregularity at one level would compound as the structure rose, pulling the tower out of shape. The builders had no measuring instruments beyond their hands, their eyes, and the knowledge passed to them by the generation before.

At the centre of each pyramid, a vertical shaft was left open. This hollow core served two purposes. First, it allowed the structure to dry from the inside as well as the outside, reducing the risk of the interior remaining wet while the exterior hardened. Second, it was the ritual space: the place where offerings would be placed and where Ala was believed to reside.

image.note: Top-down view of pyramid showing outer stepped rings and hollow central shaft

pages.text: When the pyramid reached its intended height, a wooden stick was driven into the top. This was the final act of construction, and the most important one. The stick was not a decoration or a marker placed for outsiders. It was the sign that the structure was now inhabited. Ala had taken residence at the summit.

The materials that made the Nsude pyramids possible were also the materials that made them vulnerable. Mud and clay, no matter how carefully packed, cannot resist heavy rain indefinitely. Each rainy season, water would soften the walls, erode the surface, and eat into the steps. After every rainy season, the community would inspect the pyramids and begin repairs. Damaged sections were removed. New earth and clay were pressed into place. The surface was smoothed.

This cycle of erosion and renewal was understood and accepted. The pyramids were not designed to outlast their builders. They were designed to be tended, to require the attention and labour of each new generation as a condition of their continued existence. This is, in many ways, a more sophisticated relationship with a monument than building something in stone and walking away from it. The Nsude approach demanded continued engagement.

The skill required to build in this way should not be underestimated. Engineering a stable circular structure that rises in consistent steps, using only earth and clay and human hands, with no mortar and no written instructions, only knowledge held in memory and transmitted through practice, is a remarkable achievement. The Nsude pyramids are proof of mastery: of material, of form, and of the accumulated knowledge of a community working across generations.

image.note: Close-up detail of mud wall surface showing texture of hand-pressed clay with grass binding visible

pages.text: Comparing the construction methods of Nsude with those of Egypt is instructive. The Egyptian pyramids were built from limestone blocks, some weighing several tonnes, moved by teams of workers using ramps and sledges. Their scale is almost unimaginable. The Nsude pyramids were built by a single community, by hand, from local earth. Their scale is modest. But the intelligence behind their construction, the understanding of form, materials, and purpose, is no less real.

What they share is this: in both cases, a community decided that a sacred purpose required a physical form. They looked at the materials available to them. They developed the knowledge to shape those materials into something lasting. And they built. The Egyptian pyramids have lasted because stone lasts. The Nsude pyramids have not lasted. But that was never the intention. They were meant to be renewed.
Cross-reference: What has happened to the Nsude pyramids today? See Chapter Four.

The Nsude pyramids, as G. I. Jones photographed them in 1935, no longer exist. This is the hardest fact in this book. It must be stated clearly. The pyramids that stood in those photographs, ten stepped mud towers on a hillside in Enugu State, have crumbled. Decades of rain, and decades without the community maintenance that kept them standing for centuries, have reduced them to low mounds of red earth.

image.note: Sketch of site today: low grass-covered mounds in open ground with faint outlines of where pyramids stood

pages.text: How did this happen? The answer is complex, and it involves history. As colonial rule changed the social and economic life of communities across Nigeria, traditional practices were disrupted. Young people moved to cities for work and education. The collective community structure that had sustained the pyramids, the annual rebuilding, the shared responsibility, the relationship with Ala, became harder to maintain.

The colonial authorities showed no interest in preserving or studying the Nsude pyramids. The broader dismissal of African culture and history during the colonial period meant that sites like Nsude received none of the attention or resources that European or Egyptian monuments attracted. By the time Nigeria gained independence in 1960, the damage was already significant. The pyramids had not been properly maintained for many years.

What remains at Nsude today is an archaeological site, ground that holds the memory and the material of what was there. The earth itself retains traces of the structures. Archaeologists who have studied the site have been able to identify where each pyramid stood, the outline of the foundation trenches, and fragments of the compressed earth and clay that formed the walls. The site is not nothing. But it is not what it was.

Community leaders, historians, and Nigerian cultural organisations have called for the reconstruction of the Nsude pyramids. They argue that the pyramids, if rebuilt, would serve as a centre of Igbo cultural heritage, a place of education, of connection to history, and of economic benefit through tourism. The reconstruction would follow the traditional method: red earth, clay, and grass, pressed by hand. The same materials. The same form.

This raises an interesting question. Would a rebuilt Nsude pyramid be the real thing? In one sense, no. The original structures are gone, and a new pyramid would be a new creation. But in another sense, yes, because rebuilding was always how the Nsude pyramids worked. The pyramids that Jones photographed in 1935 were not the originals either. They were the version rebuilt by that generation, just as previous generations had rebuilt before them. A rebuilt Nsude pyramid would be entirely in the spirit of the original.

As knowledge of them has spread, through the photographs of G. I. Jones, the research of Nigerian archaeologists, and the interest of the Igbo diaspora around the world, they have become a symbol of something important. They are proof that pyramid-building was not a single event in human history, confined to one place and one culture. It was a form of thinking, a way of giving sacred purpose a physical shape, that emerged independently in different parts of the world.

Nigeria has pyramids. They were not built to impress conquerors. They were not built to house the bodies of kings. They were built by a community, for a goddess, from the earth of the land she governed. They were renewed every generation, because the relationship they represented needed to be renewed. And they can be renewed again.
